claims.text: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily governed by rapid formation of a robust, chromium-rich passive oxide film.
A chromium-rich passive oxide film impedes diffusion of corrosive species into the steel substrate.
Heat treatment can alter chromium distribution and thereby promote or inhibit formation of a continuous chromium oxide layer.
Passive-film thickness, integrity, composition, and continuity govern its effectiveness as a barrier to corrosive species.
Under corrosive conditions, steels with higher chromium levels develop a thin, adherent chromium oxide surface layer.
The chromium oxide layer slows further oxidation by limiting ingress of corrosive agents.
The chromium oxide layer slows metal-ion dissolution by limiting ingress of corrosive agents.
The protective effectiveness of the passive film depends on alloy composition and microstructural homogeneity.
Microstructural homogeneity minimizes localized chromium depletion.
Carbide precipitation can cause localized chromium depletion.
Steels with increased chromium content and a uniform microstructure will have lower corrosion rates than lower-chromium, non-optimized baseline steels.
Improved steels will exhibit less corrosion-related weight loss than the baseline steels.
Improved steels will exhibit higher electrochemical impedance than the baseline steels.
Improved steels will form a thicker and more uniform chromium oxide film than the baseline steels.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply in high-temperature, controlled-pressure environments containing known corrosive agents typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
Rapid thermal cycling or unforeseen aggressive species may place the system outside the proposed mechanism's domain of validity.
